NASA Lewis Research Center has extensive experience in using unstructured grids for a variety of CFD applications, including inlets, nozzles, ducts, turbomachinery, propellers, and aircraft icing.
Structured grid generators can have difficulty in meeting resolution requirements on multiple intersecting surfaces within internal flow problems.
Shock locations on the upper and lower blade surfaces of a cascade can occur at different chordwise locations, making it challenging to align the grid lines with the shock geometry.
The small gap (less than 0.2% of blade span) between rotor blades and the surrounding shroud can result in high grid skewing and a large number of grid points when attempting to model it.
Grid generation for turbine blade passages often requires multi-block grids, a large number of grid points, and a labor-intensive grid generation effort.
Rapidly varying flow passage geometries in inlet and nozzle configurations can result in difficult blocking schemes and challenges in interfacing blocks at regions of rapid geometry change.
For aircraft icing simulations, the small structures relative to the airfoil chord must be resolved, and structured grids often require an excessive number of grid points in the far-field.
The LEWICE/UE tool was used to predict the ice shape on a NACA 0012 airfoil, showing the ability to capture the complex ice growth on the airfoil surface.
NASA Lewis Research Center has in-house unstructured grid generation development activities targeted at internal flow problems.
Unstructured grids can simplify and, in some cases, enable CFD analysis of internal flow geometries with complex, changing geometries, such as ice growth on aircraft surfaces.
